To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the response of a differential delay equation to perturbations depends on the location of the pulse within the limit cycle and that the pulse can increase the period and the amplitude of oscillation.

(1) a single pulse perturbs the limit cycle solution of a differential delay equation; (2) the response depends upon the location in the limit cycle where the pulse occurs; and (3) the response can be analytically determined.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the response of a simple differential delay oscillator to perturbations of the nonlinear term.
the response of a differential delay equation to single pulse perturbations of the nonlinearity, with particular emphasis on the effect of the pulse on the limit cycle solutions.
the analysis of limit cycles of a differential delay equation with piecewise linear non-linearities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perturbed response is characterized by an initial phase shift, an amplitude increase, and an increased period, with the extent of each of these effects being dependent on the onset of the pulse.
the response of an oscillatory system to a pulse perturbation is a function of the pulse amplitude, duration and onset.

, for a given amplitude, the perturbed limit cycle is longer than the unperturbed one if the pulse onset is before the maximum and shorter than the unperturbd one if the pulse is applied after the maximum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to completely describe the response of a differential delay equation to the perturbation of a piecewise linear non-linearity with a simple pulse.

a positive pulse perturbation applied at the point of minimum of the unperturbed oscillation causes a decrease in the period and a positive pulse perturbed at the point of maximum increases the period.
the response to a single stimulus pulse can be completely characterized for a simple differential delay oscillator.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can predict the perturbed response for a pulse at a given location in the limit cycle, and we can predict how a pulse at different locations in the limit cycle will modify the response.
the response of a differential delay equation to an impulse can be analytically characterized, even for a non-smooth nonlinearity.
a single pulse perturbing the piecewise linear function at a point on the limit cycle can cause a change in the period of the limit cycles, but the change is not necessarily monotonic.
